implementation_notes: JavaScript agents are single-threaded and run every job to completion, so an object's synchronous methods are already atomic and no monitor lock is needed; the lock reappears only for async methods, where the local idiom is a promise-chain mutex - every public method queues its critical section behind the previous promise - or an explicit async-mutex library. There are no condition variables: a method that must wait for a predicate awaits a promise/event and re-checks the state, and blocking a thread is impossible on the main thread, which rules the classic monitor out entirely. Use it to serialise access to an async resource (a connection, a file, an external API) rather than to protect in-memory fields, which need no lock at all.
pitfalls: A critical section that awaits is not atomic: another job can interleave at the await, so all state must be re-checked after every await and shared invariants must be re-established.
The event loop guarantees nothing across agents: workers share memory only through SharedArrayBuffer, and Atomics.wait cannot block the main thread (there Atomics.waitAsync is the non-blocking form).
A promise-chain mutex only serialises the calls that go through it; a stray direct mutation or a missing await breaks the invariant with no error and no lock to blame.

variants.name: Shared-memory monitor with Atomics across workers
variants.idiom_name: Atomics lock word + Atomics.wait/notify on a state word
variants.implementation_notes: Across agents the only shared mutable memory is a SharedArrayBuffer, so a real monitor is built from Atomics: an Int32Array lock word acquired with a compareExchange spin (parking on Atomics.wait when it is held) is the monitor lock, and Atomics.wait on a state word plus Atomics.notify is the monitor condition. This is the one truly blocking monitor in JavaScript - available in workers, never on the main thread, where Atomics.waitAsync is the non-blocking substitute. Choose it for a worker pool sharing a table or a queue; prefer message passing (postMessage, structured clone) whenever ownership can be transferred instead of shared.
pitfalls: Atomics.wait throws where blocking is not allowed (the main thread of a browser, most embeddings), so the blocking monitor exists only inside workers.
All participants must map the same SharedArrayBuffer; a plain Array or a copied buffer silently provides no synchronisation at all, and shared memory requires cross-origin isolation in browsers.
Atomics.wait returns on timeout and on spurious wakeups - always loop on the predicate - and the lock word must be released in a finally path or the object wedges.
